name: Nouns and gender: masculine or feminine?
subtitle: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine, even a table or a street. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (il libro) and most ending in -a are feminine (la casa). Nouns ending in -e can be either. Learn each noun with its article.

concept.exampleHtml: il libro · la casa · il giornale · la chiave

qa.html: Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine: il libro, il lavoro, il documento. Nouns ending in -a are usually feminine: la casa, la strada, la visita.

Nouns ending in -e can be masculine or feminine: il pane, il giornale but la chiave, la notte. Learn them with the article. Some endings help: -zione and -tà are feminine: la stazione, la lezione, la città.
Many nouns in -ma come from Greek and are masculine: il problema, il sistema, il programma. And some short words are feminine although they end in -o: la mano, la foto, la moto, la radio.
Words from other languages that end in a consonant are usually masculine: il bar, il computer, il film, lo sport.

For people, the word often changes: il cameriere → la cameriera, il professore → la professoressa. Some words stay the same and only the article changes: il collega, la collega; il dentista, la dentista.
Only names of people and places take a capital letter: Giulia, Milano, Italia. Days, months, languages and nationalities take a small letter: lunedì, maggio, italiano.

concept.noteHtml: Common mistakes: ✗ la problema → ✓ il problema. ✗ il mano → ✓ la mano. ✗ Lunedì, Italiano in the middle of a sentence → ✓ lunedì, italiano. Before a vowel or s + consonant the article changes (l'amico, lo studente): see Articles. Next: Plurals.

items: Before a vowel, il and la become l': l'amico, l'amica.
Before s + consonant and z, masculine nouns take lo: lo studente, lo zaino.
